title: Members on society and change · AquaTerra
description: AquaTerra members write about child labour, life after war, happiness and noise, and what social impact looks like when the people doing it are teenagers.
lede: AquaTerra's members write about society and change from where they stand: as students who run community drives, and as young people watching the world around them. The pieces cover child labour, the years after a war ends, the pressure to wait for happiness, and what social impact looks like when the people doing it are teenagers.

sections.heading: what the world looks like from here
body: The Curse on Society is about child labour. It opens with a contrast: a world brimming with innovation, education, opportunity and hope, and yet millions of children still trapped in a cruel cycle of work. It asks the reader to walk down any street and notice who is working there when they should be learning.

Displacement, Speed and Time takes the same kind of question to war. It asks what happens once the fighting finally stops, and describes life after war as a complicated mix of hope and despair. The piece is a reminder that the hard part of a crisis often comes after the headlines have moved on.

sections.heading: change that teenagers can lead
body: Teen-Led NGO begins where most people would start. When you hear social impact or community drive, you probably picture suited-up adults, corporate fundraisers and large organisations. The piece asks what changes when the people running the drive are students instead. AquaTerra is student-run, and its students run the drives, so it is a question we live with every week.

The idea that change can start with a few people and a community drive runs through AquaTerra's own work. [How students run AquaTerra](/impact/student-leadership) is about how the students who run the organisation work together, and it is a good next read for anyone asking the same question as the piece.

sections.heading: the noise and the waiting
body: Lost in the Noise is about a constant feeling of loudness: notifications, opinions and expectations, and the way it becomes easy to lose track of what you believe. Chasing Happiness argues that happiness is often treated as a reward we will get later, after the exams, or once we have achieved enough or become enough.

Beyond Mortal is a short piece in sharp, broken lines about fear and being drained, and Before you Judge Read This asks us to stop before we rush to judge someone. Together these pieces ask how we pay attention to ourselves and to each other. If that sounds right, [how a drive works](/impact/how-a-drive-works) shows what one small step looks like in practice.

learnings: Social problems such as child labour and life after war do not end when the news moves on, so a drive is a start rather than a finish.
Social impact can be led by students in their own communities, not only by large organisations.
Noticing a problem on your own street is usually where useful work begins.
Rest matters to the people doing the work: several pieces here question constant noise and waiting for happiness.

faqs.q: What do AquaTerra members write about social change?
faqs.a: AquaTerra members write about child labour, life after war, the pressure to wait for happiness, the noise of constant notifications, and what teen-led social impact looks like. Their pieces are on Groundwork Diaries, the students' writing on this site.

faqs.q: What is The Curse on Society about?
faqs.a: The Curse on Society is a piece by an AquaTerra member about child labour. It contrasts a world full of innovation, education and opportunity with millions of children still trapped in work, and asks readers to notice it on any street.

AquaTerra is one example. It is a student-run registered charitable trust, open to members aged 14 to 19, and its students run the drives themselves. Teen-Led NGO, one of the Groundwork Diaries pieces, writes about that idea from the inside.

No. AquaTerra takes no monetary donations and charges no fees. It is self-funded through its own student-run events, and [how we fund the work](/impact/how-we-fund-the-work) explains how that happens.

faqs.q: How can I join AquaTerra and help with these issues?
faqs.a: AquaTerra is free to join for students aged 14 to 19. Sign in with Google, wait for an approval, and you can take part in drives across Kolkata. [Join AquaTerra](/join) to start.
